questions.question: What is event delegation and how does it work?
questions.title: Event delegation
questions.direct_answer: Event delegation places one listener on a stable ancestor and uses a bubbling event's target to identify the matching descendant interaction. It handles current and later-added children without registering a separate listener on each child.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of bubbling, target matching, and stable component ownership.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Checking only event.target and missing clicks on nested elements inside the intended control.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Delegation requires a useful propagating event and careful scoping; not every event crosses every DOM or shadow boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Register one listener on a stable ancestor.
Let a bubbling event reach that ancestor.
Use target.closest() to find the intended descendant control.
Confirm the match belongs to the ancestor before acting.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Event delegation means placing one event listener on a stable parent instead of placing a listener on every child. When a child interaction bubbles to the parent, the parent reads the event target and decides which child action should run.

Imagine a task list where each row has a remove button. A click may begin on an icon inside that button. The same click bubbles to the list, so the list listener can find the nearest element with `data-remove` and then remove the matching row.

The important lines are `event.target.closest(...)` and the containment check. `closest` handles nested markup, while `list.contains(remove)` stops the search from escaping the component. The full runnable example remains in the deep dive.

Delegation is useful for lists, menus, tables, and other components whose children are numerous or created later. The parent listener remains in place when rows are added or replaced, so listener setup does not have to follow every child lifecycle.

It is not automatically better for every control. The event must propagate in a useful way, the selector must stay local to one component, and a very large delegated handler can become hard to follow. For one or two fixed controls, direct listeners may be clearer.

sections.title: Move the listener to the owner
sections.content: The ancestor does not receive a special delegated event. It receives the same bubbling event that began at a descendant. Delegation becomes a pattern only when the ancestor interprets `target` or the composed path and maps that origin to a child action.

sections.title: Dynamic content is the clearest benefit
sections.content: A renderer can replace or append list items while the parent listener remains registered. That avoids synchronizing listener setup with every item lifecycle. The trade-off is central dispatch logic: a very large handler with many selectors can become a hidden router, so actions should stay local to one component and return early when no relevant control matches.

sections.title: Delegated click flow
sections.content:
click on icon
     ↓ bubbles with target = icon
stable list listener
     ↓ target.closest('[data-remove]')
remove button
     ↓ closest('li')
owned task row

questions.question: What is the difference between event.target and event.currentTarget?
questions.title: event.target versus event.currentTarget
questions.direct_answer: event.target is the object where the event was dispatched and remains that target during propagation. event.currentTarget is the object whose listener is currently running, so it changes as the same event reaches listeners on different nodes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of event origin versus listener ownership.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using currentTarget to identify a delegated child, or trusting target to have the child control's attributes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Retargeting across a shadow boundary can make the visible target differ from the deepest internal origin.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: target identifies the event's dispatch target.
currentTarget identifies the node whose listener is executing.
target stays stable along the visible path; currentTarget follows each listener.
Delegation normally starts from target and resolves a child with closest().

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`event.target` identifies where the event was dispatched. `event.currentTarget` identifies the object whose listener is running at that moment. They can be the same for a direct listener, but they are usually different in a delegated handler.

If a button sits inside a toolbar and the toolbar owns the listener, clicking the button gives `target = button` and `currentTarget = toolbar`. Clicking an icon inside the button may give `target = icon`, but `currentTarget` is still the toolbar.

Delegated code starts from `target` because that is where the interaction began. It uses `closest('button')` to resolve nested markup, then uses `currentTarget` to confirm that the button belongs to the listener's component.

The event target is an `EventTarget`, so code should not assume that element methods always exist. Check that it is an `Element` before calling `closest`. Shadow DOM can also retarget an event for outside listeners; `composedPath()` is available when code truly needs the permitted propagation path.

beats.recallRule: Target tells where the event came from; currentTarget tells which listener is handling it now.

sections.title: Origin and ownership are independent
sections.content: A listener can run far away from the node where an interaction began. Target keeps the visible origin attached to the event; currentTarget tells the callback which registration caused it to run. Separating these concepts is what makes both propagation logging and delegation understandable.

sections.title: Why closest is better than a direct class check
sections.content: Users click the deepest painted element under the pointer. Adding an icon or span inside a button can therefore change target without changing the control's meaning. `closest('[data-action]')` walks from that nested node to the semantic control. A containment check then prevents the upward search from escaping the component root.

sections.content:
button (target)
  └─ toolbar listener: target = button, currentTarget = toolbar
       └─ document listener: target = button, currentTarget = document
